cards.front: A {{c1::solute}} is any substance dissolved in water, such as salt or sugar.
cards.quote: A solute is any substance dissolved in water, such as salt or sugar.

cards.front: With no energy spent, which way does water move on balance across a cell membrane, and why?
cards.back: On balance toward the side with more dissolved particles that cannot cross, because each drop there holds fewer water molecules.
cards.quote: it moves toward the side with more dissolved particles that cannot cross, because each drop there holds fewer water molecules.

cards.front: Phospholipids in the cell membrane are fat-like molecules with a water-loving {{c1::head}} and two fatty tails that avoid water.
cards.back: They form two rows: a double layer.
cards.quote: fat-like molecules with a water-loving head and two fatty tails that avoid water

cards.front: A cell membrane is {{c1::selectively permeable}}: some substances cross easily and others hardly at all.
cards.quote: It is selectively permeable: some substances cross easily and others hardly at all.

cards.front: Why is the cell membrane described as flexible rather than a wall?
cards.back: Its lipids and proteins drift sideways within the double layer, as fused mouse and human cells showed.
cards.quote: The parts drift sideways, as the fused mouse and human cells showed, so the membrane is flexible, not a wall.

cards.front: How does the cell membrane take part in cell communication?
cards.back: Receptor proteins on its surface bind signal molecules from outside, such as many hormones, and set off a response inside the cell.
cards.quote: Receptor proteins on the surface bind signal molecules from outside, such as many hormones, and set off a response inside the cell.

cards.front: What lets cells tell their own kind from others, and which body system relies on it?
cards.back: Chains of sugar attached to surface proteins and lipids act like name tags. The immune system relies on this recognition.
cards.quote: Chains of sugar attached to surface proteins and lipids act like name tags.

cards.front: A {{c1::concentration gradient}} is a difference in how concentrated a substance is between two places.
cards.quote: concentration gradient, the first film's difference in concentration between two places
cards.section: Explain: moving downhill with no energy

cards.front: What is passive transport, and what are its three forms?
cards.back: Movement across a membrane down a gradient that needs no energy from the cell. Its forms are diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis.
cards.quote: Passive transport is movement across a membrane down a concentration gradient
cards.section: Explain: moving downhill with no energy

cards.front: In facilitated diffusion, how do channel proteins and carrier proteins differ?
cards.back: Channel proteins form water-friendly tunnels. Carrier proteins grab a molecule and change shape to pass it across. Both move substances from high to low.
cards.quote: Channel proteins form water-friendly tunnels, and carrier proteins grab a molecule and change shape to pass it across.
cards.section: Explain: moving downhill with no energy

cards.front: Glucose is more concentrated outside a cell and enters through carrier proteins. Does the cell spend ATP to bring it in? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. This is facilitated diffusion: glucose still moves from high to low concentration, so it is passive and needs no energy from the cell.
cards.quote: Glucose enters many of your cells by carriers, still moving from high to low.
cards.section: Explain: moving downhill with no energy

cards.front: {{c1::Osmosis}} is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
cards.back: Much of it goes through protein water channels.
cards.quote: net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane
cards.section: Explain: moving downhill with no energy

cards.front: Why do mainly solutes that cannot easily cross the membrane, such as salt, count for osmosis?
cards.back: A solute that crosses freely spreads until it is even on both sides, so it leaves no lasting difference in water.
cards.quote: A solute that crosses freely spreads until it is even on both sides and leaves no lasting difference in water.

cards.front: Compared with the inside of a cell, a {{c1::hypotonic}} solution outside has less trapped solute.
cards.back: hyper- = more, hypo- = less, iso- = the same.
cards.quote: hyper- means more, hypo- means less, iso- means the same

cards.front: A plant cell and a red blood cell both sit in distilled water, and both are saltier inside. Water enters each one. What stops it, if anything?
cards.back: The plant cell presses on its stiff wall and the wall presses back (turgor pressure), stopping net entry. The red blood cell has no wall, so it swells and may burst.
cards.why: Turgor stops net entry even though the plant cell is still saltier inside; water still crosses both ways.
cards.quote: A red blood cell has no wall, so it swells until it may burst.

cards.front: Lettuce leaves are sprinkled with salt, making the solution outside their cells hypertonic. What happens to the leaf cells, and why?
cards.back: They lose water and wilt. Water moves out toward the saltier side, so the cells lose turgor. In strong salt the membrane pulls away from the wall.
cards.quote: Loses turgor and wilts, like salted lettuce; in strong salt the membrane pulls away from the wall

cards.front: A red blood cell sits in an isotonic solution. Has water stopped crossing its membrane?
cards.back: No. Water crosses both ways equally, so there is no net movement and the cell keeps its shape.
cards.quote: None; water crosses both ways equally

cards.front: Why does drinking seawater leave a person more dehydrated, not less?
cards.back: Two steps. Absorbed salt makes the fluid around cells saltier, which can draw water out of them by osmosis. And the kidneys can only make urine less salty than seawater, so removing the salt takes more water than was drunk.
cards.quote: your kidneys can only make urine less salty than seawater, so getting rid of the extra salt takes more water than you drank

cards.front: What does active transport do that passive transport cannot, and what usually pays for it?
cards.back: It moves substances against their gradient, or carries big loads in vesicles. It uses the cell's energy, often from ATP.
cards.quote: Key idea: Active transport uses energy, often from ATP, to move substances against their gradient or to carry big loads in vesicles by endocytosis and exocytosis.

cards.front: A living animal cell keeps sodium much higher outside and potassium much higher inside. What must the cell spend to hold these differences?
cards.back: Energy: active transport (pumps), often paid for with ATP, moves substances uphill against their gradient.
cards.quote: A living animal cell, though, keeps sodium much higher outside and potassium much higher inside. The second film shows what holding those differences costs.

cards.front: {{c1::Endocytosis}} brings material into the cell.
cards.back: The membrane folds inward around it and pinches off as a vesicle inside the cell.
cards.quote: Endocytosis brings material into the cell.

cards.front: How does exocytosis release material from a cell?
cards.back: A vesicle joins the cell membrane and spills its contents outside. Like endocytosis, it needs energy.
cards.quote: A vesicle joins the cell membrane and spills its contents outside.

cards.front: A white blood cell meets a bacterium far too big for any channel or pump. How can it take the bacterium in, and does that cost energy?
cards.back: By endocytosis: the membrane folds around the bacterium and pinches off as a vesicle inside. Yes, carrying loads in vesicles needs energy.
cards.quote: Some white blood cells engulf bacteria this way.

cards.front: In the Open University demonstration, a cucumber slice in salty water went from 26 g to 23 g after 2 hours. What was its percent change in mass?
cards.back: 100 × (23 − 26) ÷ 26 = −11.5%. The slice lost about 11.5% of its mass.
cards.quote: percent change in mass = 100 × (final mass − starting mass) ÷ starting mass

cards.front: Overnight, the distilled-water cucumber slice gained 8 g and the salty slice lost 5 g. Why is percent change a fairer comparison than grams?
cards.back: The slices started at different masses (22 g and 26 g). Percent change scales each change to its own starting mass: +36.4% and −19.2%.
cards.quote: Why is percent change a fairer way to compare them than grams?

cards.front: Can the cucumber demonstration (one slice in salty water, one in distilled water) find the salt concentration at which a slice neither gains nor loses mass? Explain.
cards.back: No. The salt concentration was never reported, only two liquids were used, and there was one slice each. You would need a range of known concentrations with repeated slices.
cards.quote: the salt was added as two spoonfuls with no concentration reported, and there was one slice for each liquid

cards.front: You plan to find the sugar concentration at which potato pieces neither gain nor lose mass. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and the control.
cards.back: Independent: sucrose concentration. Dependent: percent change in mass of each piece. Control: the 0.0 mol/L dish of distilled water, with no added sugar.
cards.why: Keep constant one potato, same-size pieces, solution volume, temperature, soaking time and blotting; use at least three pieces per solution.
cards.quote: Control: the 0.0 mol/L dish of distilled water, with no added sugar.

cards.front: Potato pieces in made-up data change mass by a mean of +3% in 0.2 M sugar and −6% in 0.4 M. Drawing a straight line between these points, estimate where the change is zero.
cards.back: Zero lies 3/9 of the way from 0.2 to 0.4 M: 0.2 + 0.2 × 3 ÷ 9 ≈ 0.27 M. There water neither enters nor leaves on balance.
cards.quote: Analysis: plot mean percent change against concentration and find where the line crosses zero, between a gain and a loss.

cards.front: The zero point of a potato osmosis test does not measure exactly how much is dissolved inside the potato cells. Why not?
cards.back: The cells' turgor pressure against their walls also affects how much water they take in, so the zero point reflects wall push as well as dissolved solute.
cards.quote: It does not measure exactly what is dissolved inside them, because their turgor pressure against their walls also affects how much water they take in.

cards.front: The Chesapeake Bay's mouth averages 25 to 30 parts per thousand of salt; its head is below 0.5. A cell in balance with water at the mouth is moved to the head. Is the new water hypertonic, isotonic or hypotonic, and which way does water move?
cards.back: Hypotonic: the water outside holds far less trapped solute than the cell, so on balance water moves into the cell.
cards.quote: The Chesapeake Bay Program describes its head and tidal rivers as below 0.5 parts per thousand of salt
